plain_title: What the label means, and why it's controversial
one_liner: Long-standing patterns in how a person thinks, feels, and relates to others that cause lasting distress or trouble.
in_simple_words: Everyone has a personality: habits of thinking, feeling, and relating. A personality disorder is diagnosed when those patterns are rigid, start by early adulthood, show up across many situations, and cause real distress or problems. The DSM groups ten types into three clusters. The labels are controversial: they've been used to dismiss people, especially those with trauma histories, and especially women. What's not controversial any more is that these difficulties are treatable, and people get better.
what_it_can_feel_like: Being told I had a personality disorder felt like being told I was broken as a person. Then I found a therapist who explained it as patterns, not a verdict.
The label got me turned away from services for years. The right team used it to get me the right therapy.
I'm not my diagnosis. It describes some of my struggles. It doesn't describe me.
common_signs: Rigid patterns of thinking, feeling, and relating that cause problems across life
Starting in adolescence or early adulthood and lasting for years
Distress for the person, or repeated trouble in relationships, work, or self-image
Not explained by another condition, a substance, or a medical illness

myths_vs_facts.myth: A personality disorder means something is wrong with who you are.
myths_vs_facts.fact: It describes patterns of coping that usually developed for understandable reasons, often in response to early adversity, and that can change.
Several therapies have strong evidence, especially for borderline personality disorder. Most people improve substantially over time.

myths_vs_facts.myth: People with personality disorders are manipulative or dangerous.
myths_vs_facts.fact: This stigma causes real harm, including in healthcare. Most people with these diagnoses are struggling, not scheming, and are far more likely to be hurt than to hurt.

how_common.plain: About 1 in 10 adults meets criteria for some personality disorder in a given year, by US survey estimates. How the label is used varies a lot between countries.
how_common.figure: 9.1% of US adults with any personality disorder in the past year (NCS-R)

what_helps.plain_summary: Treatment is mainly psychological and longer-term. For borderline personality disorder, several structured therapies work well. For other types, evidence is thinner but therapy that builds self-understanding, emotional skills, and relationships helps. Medication isn't a treatment for personality disorder itself, though it may be used for depression, anxiety, or crisis symptoms, prescribed and monitored by a doctor. Consistent, respectful care relationships matter as much as the technique. Services that turn people away because of the label are going against guidelines.
evidence_based_options: Structured psychological therapies, especially for borderline personality disorder (DBT, MBT, schema therapy, transference-focused therapy)
Longer-term therapy focused on self-understanding, emotions, and relationships
Treatment of co-occurring depression, anxiety, or substance use
Crisis plans and consistent care relationships
self_help_that_supports_care: Reading about your diagnosis from sources written with people who have it
Peer support with others who share the experience
Learning emotional-regulation skills, even outside formal therapy
Knowing your rights if a service tries to exclude you because of the label

when_to_reach_out: Do long-standing patterns in how you treat yourself and others keep causing pain, broken relationships, or crises? A full assessment can help. So can a therapist who works with personality difficulties. If you're in crisis or thinking about ending your life, use the crisis strip now.
is_not: Having strong traits, being difficult sometimes, or going through a bad patch isn't a personality disorder. Trauma, autism, ADHD, and mood disorders can look similar. They are often wrongly labelled as personality disorders.
hope_note: People with these diagnoses recover. They build stable lives and relationships, and often become the wisest supporters of others.

content_notes: All personality disorder cards are flagged for clinician review because of stigma risk.

in_young_people: These disorders are rarely diagnosed before 18, because personality is still forming. Teens with intense emotional struggles can get early help without a label. That's usually the better route.
across_cultures: What counts as 'odd' or 'excessive' depends on culture. The diagnosis is used far more in some countries than others, and clinicians are advised to consider cultural context before applying it.

sub_sections.title: Cluster A: odd or eccentric
sub_sections.text: Paranoid, schizoid, and schizotypal personality disorders.

sub_sections.title: Cluster B: dramatic, emotional, or erratic
sub_sections.text: Antisocial, borderline, histrionic, and narcissistic personality disorders.

sub_sections.title: Cluster C: anxious or fearful
sub_sections.text: Avoidant, dependent, and obsessive-compulsive personality disorders.

sub_sections.title: Personality change due to another medical condition; other specified and unspecified personality disorder
